stories.title: Build an AI software factory with seven specialized agents
stories.summary: Turn one product brief into reviewed, tested, releasable software by assigning seven agents clear roles and making every handoff an artifact. This practical setup uses isolated worktrees, dependency-aware tasks, explicit quality gates, and a human-controlled release step.
stories.whyItMatters: Multi-agent systems fail when every agent edits everything or communicates only through chat. Role boundaries, durable artifacts, and automated gates make parallel work understandable, recoverable, and safe enough to reuse.
whatToWatch: Start with one small vertical slice before allowing parallel implementation
Give each agent one owned scope and require evidence with every handoff
Keep deployment, secrets, destructive operations, and final approval human-controlled
questions: Which repository workflow should you automate first?
What checks must pass before an agent can hand work to the next stage?
Which actions in your environment must always require human approval?

How to Build a Software Factory with Claude Code: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Development

tutorial.outcome: A working seven-agent pipeline that takes a scoped issue through architecture, implementation, verification, review, and a human-approved release.
prerequisites: A Git repository with a repeatable build and test command
An agent-capable coding CLI with permission limited to the repository
A task tracker or structured state store for dependencies and status
CI checks that can block merging when tests, types, lint, or security checks fail

steps.title: Turn the request into an executable brief
steps.instruction: Collect the user outcome, constraints, non-goals, edge cases, and measurable acceptance criteria. Refuse to proceed when a product decision changes behavior and has no answer.
steps.deliverable: brief.md or an issue containing scope, acceptance criteria, non-goals, and open decisions.
steps.prompt: Convert this request into a one-page implementation brief. Separate facts, assumptions, open decisions, acceptance criteria, and non-goals. Do not propose code yet.

steps.title: Map the system and contracts
steps.instruction: Inspect the repository, identify affected components and data contracts, find existing patterns to reuse, and document risks. Define interfaces before implementation details.
steps.deliverable: A change map listing files, APIs, schemas, dependencies, migrations, and rollback concerns.
steps.prompt: Read the brief and repository. Produce the smallest architecture that satisfies it, identify existing helpers to reuse, and list every contract that must remain backward compatible.

steps.title: Build a dependency-aware task graph
steps.instruction: Split the architecture into independently owned tasks. Mark dependencies, expected files, completion evidence, and integration order. Parallelize only tasks that do not edit the same surface.
steps.deliverable: A task graph with owners, dependencies, file scopes, and verification commands.
steps.prompt: Create executable tasks from the architecture. Each task must have one owner, a non-overlapping file scope, dependencies, a definition of done, and an exact verification command.

steps.title: Implement in an isolated worktree
steps.instruction: Create a branch or worktree for one ready task, make surgical changes, follow repository conventions, and commit only owned files. Return the diff, assumptions, and command results.
steps.deliverable: A focused commit with code, tests, and a short handoff containing evidence.
steps.prompt: Own only this task and file scope. Implement the complete behavior, add focused tests, run the listed checks, and return the commit SHA plus any assumptions or remaining risks.

steps.title: Prove behavior independently
steps.instruction: Test the acceptance criteria rather than trusting the implementation report. Exercise success, failure, malformed input, concurrency, persistence, and upgrade paths that apply.
steps.deliverable: A verification report with commands, observed results, and reproducible failures.
steps.prompt: Treat the implementation as untrusted. Verify every acceptance criterion and the highest-risk edge cases. Report only reproducible failures with exact commands and evidence.

steps.title: Review correctness and security
steps.instruction: Review the actual diff and surrounding call paths for logic errors, security boundaries, data loss, compatibility, and missing cleanup. Ignore style unless it creates risk.
steps.deliverable: A short list of high-confidence findings, each tied to a file, line, impact, and fix.
steps.prompt: Review this diff against the brief and repository contracts. Find only high-confidence correctness, security, compatibility, or data-loss issues. Explain impact and the smallest safe fix.

steps.title: Integrate, release, and observe
steps.instruction: Rebase onto the target branch, rerun gates on the integrated result, produce release notes and a rollback plan, then pause for human approval before merge or deployment. After release, check health and error signals.
steps.deliverable: A merge-ready change, release checklist, rollback command, and post-release observation report.
steps.prompt: Prepare the integrated release candidate. Re-run all required gates, summarize user-visible changes and risks, provide rollback steps, and stop before merge or deployment until a human approves.

qualityGates: No task starts without acceptance criteria and an owned file scope
No handoff is accepted without a diff or artifact plus command evidence
No merge occurs when required tests, type checks, lint, or security checks fail
The verifier and reviewer must not be the implementation agent
Deployment and destructive actions require explicit human approval
costControls: Use a smaller model for discovery, planning, and routine verification; reserve stronger models for architecture and difficult reviews
Cap retries and stop agents that repeat the same failed approach
Pass focused files and artifacts instead of the entire conversation
Parallelize independent tasks only; duplicate agents reviewing the same scope waste tokens
Record per-task runtime and token cost so expensive stages can be redesigned

stories.title: OpenAI's super PAC reportedly funding AI-generated news site attacking its critics
stories.summary: A report circulating on Hacker News alleges that a super PAC backed by OpenAI is funding an AI-generated news site that publishes attacks on people critical of the AI industry. The claim, as described in the shared source, points to a blurring of lines between political spending, media production, and AI-generated content used for reputational combat.
stories.whyItMatters: If accurate, this would mark one of the more direct examples of an AI lab using its political and financial muscle to shape the narrative around AI policy and its own critics, raising fresh questions about disclosure and influence.
whatToWatch: Whether OpenAI or the PAC in question issues any confirmation or denial
Whether other outlets independently verify the funding chain and the site's AI-generated content
Any regulatory or journalistic scrutiny of AI-generated political messaging
questions: Who specifically funds and operates the news site, and is the AI-generation claim verifiable?
Which critics or topics are being targeted, and to what end?

sources.title: OpenAI's super PAC is funding AI-generated news site attacking industry critics

stories.title: MiniMax ships H3 with open weights, native audio, and 2K video — day-0 support in ComfyUI
stories.summary: MiniMax has released H3, a new open-weight model that reportedly supports native audio generation and 2K video output, with day-one integration into ComfyUI. The release gives the open-source generative media community immediate hands-on access rather than waiting for third-party ports.
stories.whyItMatters: Open-weight releases with day-0 tooling support lower the barrier for developers to experiment with high-end audio/video generation outside the closed labs, intensifying competition in generative media.
whatToWatch: Community benchmarks comparing H3's video/audio quality to closed competitors
Adoption speed within the ComfyUI ecosystem
Any licensing restrictions on commercial use of the open weights
questions: What are the compute requirements for running H3 locally versus in the cloud?
How does H3's audio-video synchronization compare to established players like Runway or Pika?

stories.title: Cloudflare details running Kimi and GLM models at scale
stories.summary: Cloudflare published a technical post on serving the open-weight Kimi and GLM models — smaller, faster, and safer, according to the piece's framing — likely as part of its inference infrastructure offerings. The post appears aimed at developers looking to deploy these Chinese-origin open models in production.
stories.whyItMatters: Major infrastructure providers offering turnkey hosting for open Chinese models signals growing mainstream demand for alternatives to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models, especially on cost and openness grounds.
whatToWatch: Pricing and performance benchmarks Cloudflare publishes for Kimi/GLM versus other hosted models
Whether other infrastructure providers follow with similar open-model hosting pushes
questions: What specific optimizations make these deployments 'smaller, faster, safer' compared to standard serving?
How does Cloudflare handle any export or compliance concerns tied to Chinese-origin models?

stories.summary: OpenAI published an engineering account of how it built a realtime system intended to make voice AI more responsive, describing the effort as a six-month project. The post is framed as a technical retrospective rather than a product announcement.
stories.whyItMatters: Latency and responsiveness remain key differentiators for conversational AI products; insight into how OpenAI approached this problem signals where voice-assistant competition is heading.
whatToWatch: Whether the underlying techniques surface in ChatGPT's voice mode or the Realtime API
Any benchmarks OpenAI shares comparing latency before and after
questions: What specific bottlenecks took six months to solve?

stories.title: Researchers question whether recent SQLite 'critical' CVEs are legitimate or AI-generated noise
stories.summary: A research post examines a batch of SQLite CVEs flagged as critical, asking whether they reflect real vulnerabilities or are 'LLM slop' — likely referring to low-quality, possibly AI-generated vulnerability reports submitted without proper verification. The piece appears to be a critical look at the growing volume of automated or AI-assisted security submissions.
stories.whyItMatters: As AI tools make it easier to mass-produce vulnerability reports, the security community faces a growing signal-to-noise problem that could erode trust in CVE databases and waste maintainer time.
whatToWatch: Whether CVE maintainers or SQLite developers respond directly to the disputed entries
Any broader policy changes to CVE submission vetting in response to AI-generated reports
questions: How many of the disputed CVEs, if any, are eventually confirmed as genuine?
Is there evidence tying the questionable reports to a specific AI tool or workflow?

sources.title: SQLite Critical CVEs or LLM Slop?

stories.title: Essay argues LLMs disproportionately reward existing expertise
stories.summary: A blog post titled 'LLMs reward expertise' circulated on Hacker News, apparently arguing that people who already have deep domain knowledge get more value out of LLM assistance than novices do. No further detail beyond the title and source is available.
stories.whyItMatters: If this dynamic holds broadly, it complicates the popular narrative that AI tools primarily level the playing field for less-skilled workers, instead suggesting AI could widen expertise gaps.
whatToWatch: Discussion and pushback in the Hacker News comments testing the essay's central claim
questions: What evidence or examples does the essay use to support its argument?
Does the claim hold across different domains, or is it specific to certain kinds of expertise?

stories.title: Blog post argues developers should retype LLM-generated code by hand to avoid 'cognitive debt'
stories.summary: A personal blog post suggests manually retyping code generated by LLMs as a way to prevent what it calls 'cognitive debt' — a loss of understanding or skill from passively accepting AI output. It's an individual opinion piece rather than a study or product announcement.
stories.whyItMatters: The idea reflects a growing undercurrent of concern among developers about skill atrophy and over-reliance on AI coding assistants, a debate likely to keep surfacing as agentic coding tools spread.
whatToWatch: Whether the practice gains traction as a broader recommendation among engineering teams
questions: Is there any evidence beyond anecdote that retyping code actually preserves skill or understanding?
How would this practice scale for large AI-generated codebases?
